items.title: test: key schema BDD coverage, SerDe client tests, and user guide

labels.name: testing
labels.description: Tasks to increase test coverage or test different scenarios

items.body:
> **Scope:** All tests run with `AUTH_ENABLED=false`. See #336 and #337 for authenticated variants.

> **Note:** The BDD and SerDe test scenarios in this issue are illustrative examples only. They SHOULD be reanalysed and refined as part of implementation to ensure they align with actual registry behaviour, existing step definitions, and any new gaps discovered during development.

## Context

Kafka messages have two independently-schematized parts: a **key** and a **value**. The schema registry stores key and value schemas as separate subjects (e.g., `orders-key` and `orders-value` under `TopicNameStrategy`). Key schemas matter for:

- **Partitioning** — Kafka hashes the key to assign partitions; same key = same partition = ordering guarantee
- **Log compaction** — compacted topics retain only the latest value per key; the key schema defines identity
- **Stream joins** — KStreams/ksqlDB join topics on their keys; both sides MUST share a compatible key schema
- **CDC / change capture** — Debezium and similar tools emit the primary key as the Kafka key

Yet our test suite almost exclusively tests value schemas, and we have no user-facing documentation explaining key schema patterns.

### Current coverage

| What exists | Where |
|---|---|
| MCP workflow registers `orders-key` + `orders-value` (basic happy path) | `tests/bdd/features/mcp/mcp_workflow_new_topic.feature` |
| Value-only subject naming with `-value` suffix throughout | ~50+ BDD feature files |
| Go/Java/Python SerDe tests — all value-only | `tests/compatibility/go/`, `java/`, `python/` |

**Gaps:**
- No BDD tests for key schema registration, evolution, compatibility, references, or data contracts
- No SerDe client tests using key serializers/deserializers
- No documentation explaining key schema patterns, use cases, or best practices

---

## Part A: Documentation — Key Schema User Guide

### Deliverable

A comprehensive guide at `docs/guides/key-schemas.md` aimed at developers and architects who need to understand when and how to use key schemas with the schema registry.

### Required sections

**1. What Are Key Schemas and Why Do They Matter?**
- Explain the Kafka message model (key + value + headers + metadata)
- Key determines partition assignment (consistent hashing)
- Key defines record identity for log compaction
- Key enables stream processing joins (KStreams, ksqlDB, Flink)
- Key enables CDC primary key propagation (Debezium, Maxwell)
- When you DON'T need a key schema (null keys, simple string/integer keys without schema enforcement)

**2. Subject Naming Conventions**
- `TopicNameStrategy` (default): `{topic}-key` and `{topic}-value` — when to use, how it works
- `RecordNameStrategy`: key subject = fully qualified record name — use case: shared key type across topics
- `TopicRecordNameStrategy`: key subject = `{topic}-{namespace}.{name}` — use case: multiple record types per topic with topic isolation
- How to configure `key.subject.name.strategy` independently from `value.subject.name.strategy`
- Code examples in Go, Java, Python for setting each strategy

**3. Common Key Schema Patterns**

Pattern descriptions with schema examples, use cases, and trade-offs:

| Pattern | Key Schema | When to Use |
|---|---|---|
| Simple string key | `{"type":"string"}` | Most common; topic-level partitioning, no compaction semantics |
| Simple integer key | `{"type":"long"}` | Auto-increment IDs, sensor IDs |
| Composite key | Record with multiple fields (e.g., `tenant_id` + `entity_id`) | Multi-tenant partitioning, compound identity |
| Enum key | Enum type (e.g., region, category) | Fixed cardinality partitioning |
| Null key (no schema) | No key subject registered | Round-robin partitioning, no compaction, no joins |
| Same type as value key | Same record type used for both | CDC / Debezium patterns (primary key record) |
| Shared key across topics | Same key schema referenced by multiple topics | Stream joins between topics |

For each pattern, include:
- Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema examples of the key schema
- When this pattern is appropriate
- Partitioning and compaction implications
- Code snippet showing producer configuration in Go, Java, Python

**4. Key Schema Best Practices**

- **Use `FULL` or `FULL_TRANSITIVE` compatibility for key schemas** — removing or renaming key fields breaks partitioning and compaction. Value schemas can be more permissive (`BACKWARD`), but keys SHOULD be strictly controlled.
- **Keep keys small** — keys are stored in partition index; large keys waste memory and slow down compaction
- **Avoid evolving key schemas if possible** — changing the key schema can split records across partitions. If evolution is needed, use `FULL` compatibility to prevent breaking changes.
- **Set `auto.register.schemas=false` for keys in production** — accidental key schema registration can cause partitioning surprises
- **Use `normalize.schemas=true` for keys** — ensures whitespace/ordering differences don't create duplicate schema versions
- **Tag key fields with metadata** — use `tags` to mark PII fields in keys for CSFLE or governance
- **Document key schema ownership** — use `metadata.properties.owner` to track which team owns the key contract

**5. Key Schema Evolution**

- What changes are safe under `FULL` compatibility (add optional field with default)
- What changes are unsafe (remove field, change type, renumber Protobuf fields)
- Impact of key schema evolution on existing partitioned data
- Migration strategies when key schema MUST change (new topic + reprocessing)
- How `FULL_TRANSITIVE` protects against multi-version drift

**6. Key Schemas with References**

- Avro: key record referencing a shared enum or record type (e.g., `Region` enum used in both key and value)
- Protobuf: key message importing shared `.proto` definitions
- JSON Schema: key using `$ref` to shared type
- Best practice: shared types used in keys SHOULD have `FULL` compatibility

**7. Key Schemas with Data Contracts**

- Adding metadata/tags to key schemas (e.g., PII tagging for compliance)
- CEL domain rules on key schemas (e.g., validate key field constraints)
- CSFLE on key fields (when key fields contain PII that must be encrypted — rare but valid)
- Independent rulesets: key and value rulesets are fully independent

**8. Client Configuration Reference**

Quick-reference table of all key-relevant client config properties:

| Property | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `key.serializer` / `key.deserializer` | — | Serializer class for keys (language-specific) |
| `key.subject.name.strategy` | `TopicNameStrategy` | How to derive the key subject name |
| `auto.register.schemas` | `true` | Whether to auto-register key schemas (applies to both key and value) |
| `use.latest.version` | `false` | Use latest key schema version instead of exact match |
| `normalize.schemas` | `false` | Normalize key schemas before registration |
| `id.compatibility.strict` | `true` | Verify key schema ID matches subject |

Include per-language code examples showing full producer/consumer setup with key serialization in Go, Java, Python.

**9. Troubleshooting Key Schemas**

Follow SDRR framework:
- Key schema not found (40401) — subject name strategy mismatch between producer and consumer
- Incompatible key schema (409) — trying to evolve key under strict compatibility
- Wrong partition assignment after schema change — key field changes alter hash
- Key deserialization failure — consumer using wrong schema version or strategy
- Duplicate key subjects — normalization differences creating separate subjects

### Format requirements

- RFC 2119 compliance for requirement language
- Code examples in all three languages (Go, Java, Python) using official Confluent client libraries
- Architecture diagrams: message wire format (key bytes + value bytes), partition assignment flow
- Cross-reference to `docs/guides/client-configuration.md` (from #357 task) and `docs/best-practices.md`

---

## Part B: BDD Test Coverage

### Area 1: Key Schema Registration & Lookup (BDD — P0)

> **NET NEW** — no existing coverage.

```gherkin
Feature: Key schema registration and lookup

  Scenario: Register key and value schemas independently
    Given the registry is running
    When I register schema '{"type":"string"}' for subject "orders-key" with type "AVRO"
    And I register schema for subject "orders-value" with type "AVRO":
      """
      {"type":"record","name":"Order","fields":[{"name":"id","type":"string"},{"name":"total","type":"double"}]}
      """
    Then subject "orders-key" should have 1 version
    And subject "orders-value" should have 1 version
    And the schemas should have different global IDs

  Scenario: Key and value schemas evolve independently
    Given subject "payments-key" has schema '{"type":"record","name":"PaymentKey","fields":[{"name":"txn_id","type":"string"}]}'
    And subject "payments-value" has schema '{"type":"record","name":"Payment","fields":[{"name":"amount","type":"double"}]}'
    When I register a new version of "payments-value" adding field "currency" with default "USD"
    Then subject "payments-value" should have 2 versions
    And subject "payments-key" should still have 1 version

  Scenario: List subjects returns both key and value subjects
    Given subject "users-key" exists
    And subject "users-value" exists
    When I list all subjects
    Then the response should contain "users-key"
    And the response should contain "users-value"

  Scenario: Delete key subject without affecting value subject
    Given subject "events-key" has 1 version
    And subject "events-value" has 2 versions
    When I soft-delete subject "events-key"
    Then subject "events-key" should be marked as deleted
    And subject "events-value" should still have 2 active versions

  Scenario: Register complex Avro record as key
    When I register schema for subject "user-activity-key" with type "AVRO":
      """
      {"type":"record","name":"ActivityKey","namespace":"com.example",
       "fields":[
         {"name":"user_id","type":"string"},
         {"name":"region","type":"string"}
       ]}
      """
    Then registration should succeed
    And the schema should be retrievable by its global ID

  Scenario: Register Protobuf message as key
    When I register schema for subject "sensor-key" with type "PROTOBUF":
      """
      syntax = "proto3";
      message SensorKey {
        string device_id = 1;
        string location = 2;
      }
      """
    Then registration should succeed

  Scenario: Register JSON Schema as key
    When I register schema for subject "audit-key" with type "JSON":
      """
      {"type":"object","properties":{"tenant_id":{"type":"string"},"timestamp":{"type":"integer"}},"required":["tenant_id"]}
      """
    Then registration should succeed
```

### Area 2: Key Schema Compatibility & Evolution (BDD — P0)

> **NET NEW** — no existing coverage.

```gherkin
Feature: Key schema compatibility

  Scenario: Key schema FULL compatibility prevents field removal
    Given global compatibility is "BACKWARD"
    And subject "orders-key" has compatibility level "FULL"
    And subject "orders-key" has schema '{"type":"record","name":"OrderKey","fields":[{"name":"order_id","type":"string"},{"name":"region","type":"string"}]}'
    When I register a schema for "orders-key" removing field "region"
    Then the request should fail with error code 409

  Scenario: Key schema FULL compatibility allows adding optional field with default
    Given subject "orders-key" has compatibility level "FULL"
    And subject "orders-key" has schema '{"type":"record","name":"OrderKey","fields":[{"name":"order_id","type":"string"}]}'
    When I register a schema for "orders-key" adding field "partition_hint" with default ""
    Then registration should succeed
    And subject "orders-key" should have 2 versions

  Scenario: Key and value subjects have independent compatibility levels
    Given subject "events-key" has compatibility level "FULL"
    And subject "events-value" has compatibility level "BACKWARD"
    When I GET /config/events-key
    Then the response should contain "FULL"
    When I GET /config/events-value
    Then the response should contain "BACKWARD"

  Scenario: Key schema type change rejected under FULL compatibility
    Given subject "metrics-key" has compatibility level "FULL"
    And subject "metrics-key" v1 is '{"type":"string"}'
    When I register schema '{"type":"long"}' for subject "metrics-key"
    Then the request should fail with error code 409

  Scenario: Protobuf key field renumbering rejected
    Given subject "device-key" has compatibility level "FULL" and type "PROTOBUF"
    And subject "device-key" has schema:
      """
      syntax = "proto3";
      message DeviceKey { string device_id = 1; }
      """
    When I register schema renumbering device_id to field 2
    Then the request should fail with error code 409

  Scenario: Key FULL_TRANSITIVE checks against all versions
    Given subject "tenant-key" has compatibility level "FULL_TRANSITIVE"
    And subject "tenant-key" has 3 schema versions
    When I register a v4 schema that is compatible with v3 but not v1
    Then the request should fail with error code 409
```

### Area 3: Cross-Format Key + Value Combinations (BDD — P1)

> **NET NEW** — no existing coverage.

```gherkin
Feature: Cross-format key and value schemas

  Scenario Outline: Register key and value with different schema types
    When I register a <key_type> schema for subject "mixed-key"
    And I register a <value_type> schema for subject "mixed-value"
    Then both registrations should succeed
    And subjects should be independently versioned

    Examples:
      | key_type | value_type |
      | AVRO     | PROTOBUF   |
      | AVRO     | JSON       |
      | PROTOBUF | AVRO       |
      | PROTOBUF | JSON       |
      | JSON     | AVRO       |
      | JSON     | PROTOBUF   |

  Scenario: String key with complex Avro value (most common pattern)
    When I register schema '{"type":"string"}' for subject "logs-key" with type "AVRO"
    And I register a complex record schema for subject "logs-value" with type "AVRO"
    Then both registrations should succeed

  Scenario: No key schema with value schema (null/unschematized key)
    When I register a schema for subject "notifications-value"
    And subject "notifications-key" does not exist
    Then listing subjects should contain "notifications-value"
    And listing subjects should not contain "notifications-key"
```

### Area 4: Key Schema References (BDD — P1)

> **NET NEW** — no existing coverage.

```gherkin
Feature: Key schema references

  Scenario: Avro key references a shared enum type
    Given subject "com.example.Region" has schema:
      """
      {"type":"enum","name":"Region","namespace":"com.example","symbols":["US","EU","APAC"]}
      """
    When I register schema for subject "orders-key" referencing "com.example.Region":
      """
      {"type":"record","name":"OrderKey","fields":[
        {"name":"order_id","type":"string"},
        {"name":"region","type":"com.example.Region"}
      ]}
      """
    Then registration should succeed

  Scenario: Protobuf key with import
    Given subject "common/address.proto" has a Protobuf Address message
    When I register a Protobuf key schema that imports "common/address.proto"
    Then registration should succeed
    And the key schema should list the reference

  Scenario: Key and value reference the same shared type
    Given subject "com.example.TenantId" has a shared Avro record
    When I register "multi-tenant-key" referencing "com.example.TenantId"
    And I register "multi-tenant-value" also referencing "com.example.TenantId"
    Then both should reference the same schema ID for the shared type
```

### Area 5: Key Schema Data Contracts (BDD — P1)

> **NET NEW** — no existing coverage.

```gherkin
Feature: Key schema data contracts

  Scenario: Register key schema with metadata tags
    When I register schema for "orders-key" with metadata:
      """
      {
        "schema": "{\"type\":\"record\",\"name\":\"OrderKey\",\"fields\":[{\"name\":\"order_id\",\"type\":\"string\"}]}",
        "schemaType": "AVRO",
        "metadata": {
          "properties": {"owner": "platform-team", "sensitivity": "internal"},
          "tags": {"order_id": ["PII"]}
        }
      }
      """
    Then registration should succeed
    And retrieving the schema should include the metadata

  Scenario: CEL domain rule on key schema
    When I register schema for "validated-key" with a CEL CONDITION rule validating message.order_id.size() > 0
    Then registration should succeed

  Scenario: Key and value have independent rulesets
    Given "events-key" has a CEL rule validating key fields
    And "events-value" has a different CEL rule validating value fields
    When I retrieve both schemas
    Then each should have its own independent ruleSet
```

---

## Part C: SerDe Client Tests

### Area 6: Subject Name Strategies in SerDe Clients (SerDe — P0)

> **NET NEW** — all existing SerDe tests use value serializers only.

Test scenarios per language (Go, Java, Python):

```
6.1  TopicNameStrategy key: produce with key serializer → subject "{topic}-key" created
6.2  TopicNameStrategy value: produce with value serializer → subject "{topic}-value" created
6.3  RecordNameStrategy key: produce → subject is fully qualified record name
6.4  TopicRecordNameStrategy key: produce → subject is "{topic}-{namespace}.{name}"
6.5  Key auto-registration disabled: produce with unknown key schema → error
6.6  Key use.latest.version: produce uses latest key schema version
6.7  Complex Avro record key: serialize/deserialize round-trip
6.8  Protobuf message key: serialize/deserialize round-trip
6.9  JSON Schema key: serialize/deserialize round-trip (Java/Python only)
6.10 String key with Avro value: mixed serializers on same producer
6.11 Null key handling: produce with null key, consume → null returned
6.12 Key schema evolution: produce v1 key, evolve to v2, consume both
```

Implementation: standalone produce/consume tests against the registry (no Kafka broker needed). Located in `tests/compatibility/{go,java,python}/`.

### Area 7: Key SerDe Wire Format (SerDe — P0)

> **NET NEW** — no existing key wire format tests.

```
7.1  Avro key wire format: serialized bytes start with 0x00 + 4-byte schema ID
7.2  Protobuf key wire format: magic byte + schema ID + message index + payload
7.3  Key and value use different schema IDs in same message
7.4  Deserialize key bytes with correct schema from registry
7.5  Deserialize key with evolved schema (reader uses latest, writer used v1)
7.6  Key schema ID lookup: deserializer fetches key schema by ID from registry
```

### Area 8: Key Schema Cross-Language Interop (SerDe — P1)

> **NET NEW** — depends on interop infrastructure from #357 Area 8.

| Producer | Consumer | Format | Scenario |
|----------|----------|--------|----------|
| Java | Go | Avro | Complex record key round-trip |
| Go | Python | Avro | Complex record key round-trip |
| Java | Python | Protobuf | Protobuf message key round-trip |
| Python | Java | JSON | JSON Schema key round-trip |
| Java | Go | Avro | Key schema evolution (v1 produce, v2 consume) |

---

## Priority & Checklist

### P0 — Must have
- [ ] Part A: Key schema user guide (`docs/guides/key-schemas.md`)
- [ ] Area 1: Key schema registration & lookup (BDD)
- [ ] Area 2: Key schema compatibility & evolution (BDD)
- [ ] Area 6: Subject name strategies in SerDe clients (Go, Java, Python)
- [ ] Area 7: Key SerDe wire format (Go, Java, Python)

### P1 — Should have
- [ ] Area 3: Cross-format key + value combinations (BDD)
- [ ] Area 4: Key schema references (BDD)
- [ ] Area 5: Key schema data contracts (BDD)
- [ ] Area 8: Key schema cross-language interop (SerDe)

### Dependencies

- Areas 1–5: BDD tests using existing step definitions from `tests/bdd/steps/`
- Areas 6–7: SerDe tests in `tests/compatibility/{go,java,python}/`
- Area 8: Depends on interop infrastructure from #357 Area 8
- All tests run against Docker-deployed binary per #315
- Auth variants covered by #336 and #337

### Relationships

- Related to #357 (client-side behaviors — value-focused; this issue adds key coverage)
- Related to #356 (schema modeling — tests here use complex key schemas)
- Depends on #315 (BDD tests MUST run against Docker binary)
- The user guide cross-references `docs/guides/client-configuration.md` (task on #357)

items.body:
Suivi de **#790** (PR #879), ouvert parce que le critère d'acceptation n° 2 est sorti de l'empreinte du ticket.

## Ce que #790 a livré

Le consentement RGPD donné **à la réservation** est journalisé côté serveur : `appointments.data_consent_at` (`TIMESTAMPTZ(6)`, table scopée `tenant_id`), horodaté par le serveur dans la transaction d'insertion, recopié à l'identique lors d'un report, couvert par `apps/api/test/appointments-consent.isolation-spec.ts`. La page publique `/{salon}/politique-donnees` est servie et liée depuis les deux blocs de consentement.

## Ce qui reste

**Le consentement donné à la création de compte n'est pas journalisé.** Il vit encore dans `sessionStorage` et meurt avec l'onglet : l'établissement n'a aucune preuve de consentement pour un compte client créé, alors que CDC §5.1 attend une « base légale explicite pour chaque traitement ».

L'agent de #790 n'a volontairement rien livré de ce volet plutôt que d'ajouter au contrat d'inscription un champ que l'API aurait accepté sans rien en faire — une promesse fausse. La page de politique de données le dit explicitement aujourd'hui ; cette phrase devra être reprise quand la preuve existera.

La persistance passe par `apps/api/src/modules/identity/` — `auth.controller.ts`, `auth.service.ts`, `identity.repository.ts`, `dto/auth.dto.ts` — hors de l'empreinte `api/appointments` du ticket d'origine.

## Critères d'acceptation

- [ ] Le consentement donné à la création de compte est enregistré côté serveur, avec son horodatage UTC, sur une colonne scopée `tenant_id` (migration additive)
- [ ] Le champ est porté par le contrat partagé de l'inscription, validé par le DTO, et refusé à `false`
- [ ] Un test d'isolation inter-tenant couvre la lecture de cette donnée, et un test vérifie qu'elle n'apparaît sur aucune sortie publique
- [ ] La page `/{salon}/politique-donnees` est reprise : elle n'a plus à annoncer que l'inscription ne conserve pas de preuve horodatée

## Empreinte attendue

`api/identity`, `db:schema`, `packages/shared/identity`, `web/compte`, `web/politique-donnees`

Référence : CDC §5.1 · `.claude/skills/tenant-isolation/SKILL.md` · issue #790 · PR #879

items.title: mongodb: optional native provider plugin for declarative schema management and versioned document migrations
items.body:
## Summary

Implement MongoDB as an **optional executable provider plugin** in the separate **`stokaro/ptah-mongodb-plugin`** repository, using the public provider protocol/SDK from #4204 and the semantic ownership boundaries from #4140.

Deliver declarative management of MongoDB's stored schema metadata together with explicitly authored, versioned document migrations. This is not an embedded MongoDB engine, a MongoSQL adapter, or a wrapper around another migrator.

The intended workflow is:

```text
HCL / provider-native declarations          authored document migrations
                  \                         /
                   Ptah project and history workflow
                                |
             inspect -> compare -> plan -> review -> apply -> verify
                                |
                  public provider protocol from #4204
                                |
                     ptah-plugin-mongodb
                                |
                 official MongoDB Go driver / BSON commands
```

**The plugin is not included in the default Ptah bundle.** The host retains only the data-only recognition/setup metadata allowed by #4204. No MongoDB driver, BSON implementation, concrete schema types, command builders, or planning rules enter the host module or neutral SDK.

Research snapshot: **7 October 2026**; Ptah source inspected at `a2993625f392e3dc093a2f4fb47fb50d56a231f1`. The requirements below describe a proposed implementation, not functionality already implemented or certified.

## 1. Why this belongs in Ptah

MongoDB has a flexible document model, but it also has persistent, inspectable definitions: collection options, validators, ordinary indexes, and view pipelines. Changes to those definitions and changes to existing documents are different workflows and both require controlled execution. MongoDB's native [`create`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/create/), [`collMod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/collmod/), and [index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/indexes/) APIs provide the relevant surfaces.

MongoDB's official [SQL Interface](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/sql-interface/) is read-only. Its analytical SQL schemas are not the authoritative collection validators or an interface for schema/data mutations. Do not depend on MongoSQL, JDBC/ODBC, BI Connector, `database/sql`, `mongosh`, Node.js, or an embedded JavaScript runtime.

This is not an unexplored migration category: [Liquibase's MongoDB extension](https://github.com/liquibase/liquibase-mongodb) provides modeled changes and command execution; [migrate-mongo](https://github.com/seppevs/migrate-mongo) provides authored JavaScript migrations and a changelog. The proposed value is Ptah's integrated **desired-state diff, reviewable native plans, explicit coverage, drift verification, and versioned execution**, not a claim to have invented MongoDB migrations.

Do not infer document transformations from validator differences. Tightening a validator does not tell Ptah how to repair existing application data.

## 2. Relationship to #4140 and #4204

#4140 supplies the common/native semantic boundary. #4204 supplies one provider system, local subprocess lifecycle, gRPC/Protobuf transport, neutral SDK, discovery/trust, coarse semantic calls, and history/execution contracts. **Reuse those facilities; do not create a MongoDB-specific registry, RPC protocol, planner, or history policy.**

Apply #4204's **clean-break, no-legacy policy**. Refactor affected host contracts directly, updating repository-owned consumers/tests/docs. Do not introduce old/new schema representations, legacy artifact readers, SQL-shaped compatibility facades, or an embedded fallback. Compatibility guarantees for the new stable protocol still apply from its v1 release onward.

### A native-only provider, not a second core

MongoDB must work when the schema contains **zero relational tables, columns, or SQL AST statements**. Represent MongoDB resources through the generic native-object/change/execution envelopes. Do not add a parallel `DocumentDatabase` core or a global relational-versus-document switch to application orchestration.

| Responsibility | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| Project resolution, common HCL evaluation, source locations, generic object references and coverage | Host / neutral contracts |
| Global dependency ordering, conflicts, policy/approval, revision policy, workflow state | Host |
| Collection/index/view definitions, MongoDB validation semantics, BSON values, target normalization and equality | MongoDB plugin |
| Inspection, feature/permission probing, native plan contributions, command lowering and safety evidence | MongoDB plugin |
| Connections, transactions, MongoDB lock/history storage primitives, execution and result reconciliation | MongoDB plugin, under host orchestration |
| Human and machine-readable presentation | Common envelopes and plugin-provided structured detail; not opaque summaries alone |

The shared pipeline may understand identity, ownership, dependencies, risks and completion without understanding a validator expression. It must not pretend that MongoDB field paths are SQL columns, a MongoDB validator is SQL RLS, or MongoDB uniqueness has SQL NULL semantics.

### Audit the actual product path

At the inspected commit, [`migrationfile.DirFormat`](https://github.com/stokaro/ptah/blob/a2993625f392e3dc093a2f4fb47fb50d56a231f1/migration/migrationfile/format.go) describes SQL-based layouts and [`ParsedUp`](https://github.com/stokaro/ptah/blob/a2993625f392e3dc093a2f4fb47fb50d56a231f1/migration/migrationfile/parsed_up.go) exposes `SQL string`. An RPC command executor alone does not make versioned MongoDB migrations work.

Audit and connect native-only resources through decoding/export, inspection, empty-state/empty-diff checks, selection, comparison, ordering, lint/risk reports, migration-directory discovery, checksums, saved plans, revision storage, apply/status, verification, and applicable language-server/application consumers. Do not silently skip native files and report “no pending migrations.”

Make missing generic seams part of #4204's design rather than engine-specific exceptions. In particular, a **native-only conformance fixture should exercise the contract before its first stable freeze**. Full MongoDB delivery remains a separate dependency-consuming project, not an additional completion prerequisite for all of #4204. If the protocol has already stabilized, negotiate the required generic feature/version instead of silently weakening its contract.

Follow [ADR 0012](https://github.com/stokaro/ptah/blob/a2993625f392e3dc093a2f4fb47fb50d56a231f1/docs/adr/0012-the-canonical-core-is-removed-and-the-shipping-pipeline-migrates-in-place.md): the result must run through the shipping pipeline, not a disconnected alternative core.

## 3. Repository, packages, and installation

The fixed repository boundary is `stokaro/ptah-mongodb-plugin`. A proposed internal layout is:

```text
stokaro/ptah-mongodb-plugin/
  go.mod
  cmd/ptah-plugin-mongodb/
  schema/                    typed native definitions and changes
  internal/codec/            source codecs, ordered BSON, canonical projections
  internal/inspect/          metadata and coverage
  internal/compare/          target-aware semantic comparison
  internal/plan/             contributions, lowering, preconditions and risks
  internal/execute/          sessions, commands, progress and reconciliation
  internal/backend/          lock and revision storage primitives
  internal/capability/       version / FCV / topology / deployment facts
  tests/                     conformance, integration, failure and packaging tests
  docs/
```

Use the official [`go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/go/current/get-started/) module, pinned in the plugin. The plugin consumes published neutral SDK modules, not Ptah application/internal packages. It must build from a clean external checkout with `GOWORK=off` and no local `replace` directives. Build the normal plugin without CGO; optional native encryption dependencies are not implicit requirements of this delivery.

Add one data-only official-plugin catalog entry: engine ID `mongodb`, documented aliases, `mongodb://` and `mongodb+srv://`, provider identity, repository, canonical setup-documentation URL, and `bundled = false`. Publish the setup page before treating that entry as a completed deliverable.

A missing plugin must produce #4204's structured installation diagnostic **before** provider-dependent decoding, DNS/database access, provisioning or mutation when the engine is explicit. Installed-but-disabled, untrusted, incompatible and failed providers remain distinct errors. There is no fallback to SQL, another MongoDB-compatible service, or a built-in implementation, and no automatic download/enable/upgrade.

Release independently versioned, verified artifacts, manifests, checksums/provenance and SBOMs. Publish and test the actual platform matrix. Native CLI and applicable LSP/other consumers use the existing shared plugin host. Do not claim Atlas CLI/SQL compatibility for MongoDB merely because it works through Ptah's runtime; strict compatibility-mode refusals remain authoritative.

## 4. Native object model and source formats

### Typed objects with structured identity

Use provider-owned kinds, illustratively:

```text
ptah.run/mongodb/collection
ptah.run/mongodb/index
ptah.run/mongodb/view
ptah.run/mongodb/search-index       # extension workstream, not an ordinary index
```

A collection definition owns its collection options and validator state. Indexes are independently addressable child resources; views are independently addressable namespace resources. A validator has no independent MongoDB object name: do not invent a second independently managed validator resource that can conflict with the collection definition.

Keep database, collection/view name, index family and index name as separate reference components. Collections and views share a physical namespace; a different kind tag must not permit both to claim the same database/name. Do not split names on dots, lowercase them globally, or confuse a document field path with an object reference. Keep namespace identity separate from collation semantics.

Capture collection UUID as **observed identity/precondition evidence**, not portable desired state. Preserve desired versus observed distinctions and explicit managed/absent/defaulted/uninspected dispositions. Native changes carry their complete before/after operands, ownership context, dependencies and relevant evidence; do not recover missing operands from a later live read.

### BSON is a semantic requirement

Use concrete provider types for collection/index/view definitions and an ordered BSON representation for expression/pipeline fragments. The [Go driver distinguishes ordered `bson.D` from unordered `bson.M`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/go/current/data-formats/bson/). Preserve key order where meaningful, especially compound indexes, commands, sort documents, pipelines and literal embedded documents.

The codec must preserve missing versus null, integer widths, large integers, Decimal128, doubles, dates versus timestamps, ObjectId, binary subtype/UUID, regex and nested arrays/documents. Reject duplicate keys in authored definitions and malformed/oversized payloads; never silently take the last value. Unknown observed values must be preserved with coverage limitations or rejected explicitly, not coerced to strings or empty objects.

Use [Extended JSON v2](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/mongodb-extended-json/) for readable BSON-bearing input/output and a versioned provider-owned encoding inside the generic wire envelope. **Canonical Extended JSON is a type-preserving interchange format, not by itself a semantic fingerprint algorithm.** Define deterministic, versioned comparison/fingerprint projections separately. Normalize only proven equivalents: never recursively sort every BSON document or erase BSON type differences globally.

### HCL first, without an unordered BSON shortcut

Use the shared HCL evaluator and #4204's provider schema descriptors. The provider supplies its block/attribute semantics and diagnostics; it does not implement another HCL evaluator. Preserve source ranges and field paths through plugin calls.

Illustrative syntax to finalize against the SDK; this is **not a claim that the syntax already exists**:

```hcl
mongodb_collection "users" {
  validator_ejson   = file("users.validator.ejson")
  validation_level  = "strict"
  validation_action = "error"

  index "users_tenant_email" {
    key {
      path = "tenant_id"
      kind = "asc"
    }
    key {
      path = "email"
      kind = "asc"
    }
    unique = true
  }
}
```

Example `users.validator.ejson`:

```json
{
  "$jsonSchema": {
    "bsonType": "object",
    "required": ["tenant_id", "email"],
    "properties": {
      "tenant_id": { "bsonType": "string" },
      "email": { "bsonType": "string" }
    }
  }
}
```

Repeated key blocks preserve compound-key ordering; `keys = { ... }` is not an acceptable ordered representation. BSON fragments must not pass through `jsondecode`/generic maps that lose order or numeric meaning. File contents are resolved by the normal source-loading workflow and frozen into the planned artifact, not reread as different bytes at apply time.

Provide faithful HCL export and a versioned provider-native representation for schema snapshots/migration units. SQL, DBML and relational Go-model inputs must fail explicitly where they cannot express MongoDB semantics; do not invent lossy collection/table conversions. Offline decode/compare/render works without credentials or a live database, using an explicit target profile with unresolved runtime facts visible.

## 5. Functional scope and capability accounting

### Required first delivery

| Family | Required behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Ordinary collections | Inspect/export, create, explicit approved drop, options comparison; explicit same-database rename with collision/UUID checks and no implicit `dropTarget` |
| Validators | MongoDB `$jsonSchema`, supported query-expression validators and their combinations; add/change/remove; validation level/action; correct staged 9.0 constraint transitions |
| Ordinary indexes | Single/compound keys; ascending/descending, hashed, text, wildcard and supported geospatial key types; unique, sparse, partial, collation, TTL and hidden options; inspect/create/drop and legal in-place modifications |
| Standard views | Source collection/view, ordered aggregation pipeline, collation, dependencies; create/modify/drop, cycles/conflicts and unsupported-pipeline diagnostics |
| Versioned migrations | Reviewable typed schema operations plus explicitly authored bounded document mutations/assertions; checksums, history/status, recovery and verification |
| Operational workflow | Install -> connect -> inspect -> declare -> diff/plan -> apply -> inspect/no-diff; offline artifacts and missing-plugin diagnostics |

Support is measured **per operation and option combination**, not by an engine-wide boolean. Do not advertise an index family merely because its create command can be sent: inspection/normalization/export/diff and safe refusal paths must work too. Multikey behavior arises from indexed document values; do not invent a portable `multikey = true` creation option.

For each feature record supported, unsupported by MongoDB, not implemented by this provider, unavailable for the selected server/FCV/topology/deployment, permission denied, or unverified. These are different dispositions. Runtime probing is read-only; an authorization failure is not proof that a feature does not exist.

Target **pinned MongoDB 8.0 and 9.0 release lines** for initial integration evidence, with exact patch versions, driver versions and FCVs recorded at implementation time. Include standalone and replica-set fixtures with explicit transaction differences. Test lower-FCV/version rejection independently. These are proposed certification targets, not claims that tests have already passed. Other release lines require declared evidence rather than extrapolation.

MongoDB [9.0 was released on 29 September 2026](https://www.mongodb.com/products/updates/mongodb-9-0-is-now-available/). Do not base the provider on an outdated assumption that validators only have the older levels.

### Explicit extension boundary, not silent feature loss

| Area | Disposition for this issue |
| --- | --- |
| Capped, clustered and time-series collections | Recognize, inspect/export or report exact incomplete coverage, and preserve. Full lifecycle/alteration support is a separately scoped extension; never treat them as ordinary collections. |
| Search / Vector Search indexes | Separate native-object extension workstream described below. Distinct from ordinary/text indexes; do not claim complete index coverage from `listIndexes`. |
| Sharding, shard keys, zones, resharding, balancing | Out of first-delivery mutation scope. Detect topology and refuse unsupported mutation workflows rather than operate directly on a shard as if standalone. |
| Users/roles, Atlas projects/clusters, backup policies | Separate security/control-plane scope; no automatic account or cloud-resource management. |
| Queryable/client-side encryption, key vaults and internal state collections | Recognize/protect relevant state; no implicit encryption/key-management support or destructive rebuild. |
| Change-stream subscriptions, application CDC/catch-up and embedding generation | Not generated from schema diff; separate authored/application workflows. Collection pre/post-image settings may be added as typed capabilities, not a claim to manage consumers. |
| DocumentDB, Cosmos DB MongoDB API, FerretDB and other compatibility layers | Not certified by MongoDB wire/URI compatibility. Require explicit support profiles and tests; reject positively identified unsupported products before mutation. |

An unsupported unrelated resource should not prevent all read-only inventory or provably unrelated safe operations. It **must** block an operation whose correctness/preservation depends on understanding it, especially parent drop/recreation or cascade.

## 6. Inspection, ownership, and no-diff correctness

Use [`listCollections`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/listcollections/) for actual options, validators, collection kinds, view definitions and UUIDs, and [`listIndexes`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/listindexes/) for ordinary indexes. Exhaust cursors with bounded streaming; cancellation, a failed later batch or unreadable required fields must not become a complete empty result.

`authorizedCollections: true` together with `nameOnly: true` can expose only the namespaces accessible to the user and omit the options needed for comparison. Never use that result as a complete database snapshot. Report permission-limited coverage and the actual missing inspection capability.

Inspection does not sample documents to invent required fields, create collections/history/locks, or run mutating feature probes. Optional data-quality preflights are separately requested bounded reads, with separate permissions and explicit cost/completeness.

Define scope independently for collections, their owned indexes and relevant options. **Omitted is not automatically “delete everything else.”** Destructive authoritative management requires explicit scope and adequate coverage. Preserve unowned indexes/options; never claim complete state after discarding unknown metadata.

Protect `admin`, `local`, `config`, `system.*`, time-series buckets, recognized encryption internals, and Ptah's exact configured history/lock/checkpoint resources. Do not emit ordinary drop operations for engine-managed `_id` indexes. Explicit adoption of a managed namespace must not adopt the whole database accidentally.

Normalize effective defaults and server-generated metadata without losing source intent: inherited collation, absent versus false, absent versus TTL zero, generated index names, index-version fields, and normalized text/wildcard definitions need real round-trip tests. Document data, index-build progress and other transient runtime state must not cause perpetual schema drift.

Introspection across several commands is not automatically a point-in-time metadata snapshot. Use primary/read-consistency behavior appropriate to the supported workflow, detect relevant concurrent changes, and revalidate object UUIDs and metadata before each dependent mutation. A Ptah lock does not stop an external administrator changing the collection.

## 7. Planning and safety rules

The plugin contributes typed changes, effects, object dependencies, exact native units, preconditions, verification and transaction constraints. The host owns the final graph, policy and execution order. Pure decode/compare/plan calls must not mutate anything.

### Validators are not automatic data repair

MongoDB implements its own [JSON Schema dialect](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/jsonschema/), including `bsonType` and documented omissions. Do not validate with an unrelated generic JSON Schema dialect and assume MongoDB will interpret it identically.

Treat validator changes as possible application-compatibility or integrity changes. Conservatively distinguish tightening, weakening and unknown effects where provable; do not claim logical equivalence/implication for arbitrary MQL predicates from textual similarity.

For the older levels, switching to `strict` does **not** retroactively certify old documents. `moderate`, `off`, `warn` and validation bypass are not interchangeable safety strategies. Never silently weaken enforcement to make an apply pass.

For [MongoDB 9.0 `constraint` validation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/schema-validation/specify-validation-level/), model the documented state machine: existing-collection preparation, allowed validation actions, the full existing-data check and its cost, and restrictions on changing a validator while constrained. A rule change may require a visible temporary downgrade to `strict`, rule update, preparation and re-establishment of the constraint. That enforcement gap is an explicit plan effect requiring policy approval. Preparation is a mutation, not a read-only preflight. Failed intermediate steps must remain visible/recoverable.

For a staged application rollout, document expand -> deploy compatible writers -> bounded backfill -> verification -> contract. The application rollout and business transformation remain author responsibilities. Ptah must not infer how to split a person's name or regenerate embeddings from a schema change.

### Index changes have distinct operational and data effects

Use [`collMod`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/collmod/) only for supported in-place changes, such as TTL/hidden state and applicable unique conversion. A changed key pattern or an unsupported option change is not automatically an in-place alteration. [Index rename requires replacement](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/indexes/); replacement ordering must account for server conflicts and cannot assume old/new indexes can coexist.

For unique conversion, model `prepareUnique`, validation and completion as separate effects where used. A server dry run is specific to that supported operation, not a general MongoDB plan simulation. Never deduplicate data automatically. Enforce MongoDB's [unique-index semantics](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-unique/), including missing/null values, partial filters, collation, multikey behavior and prohibited combinations such as unique hashed indexes.

Creating TTL or reducing retention is a **potentially destructive data change**, even though represented as metadata. Expiration can delete existing documents; restoring the previous TTL does not restore them. Invalid compound-TTL combinations must be rejected rather than accepted because the server might ignore the option. See [TTL behavior](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl/).

A [hidden index](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-hidden/) still enforces uniqueness and TTL. Hiding is not disabling its integrity/deletion effects. Index builds/replacements also need explicit disk/workload/availability risk reporting; do not promise zero blocking or constant-time cancellation.

### Collection and view operations

Never silently drop/recreate a collection to change an immutable option, collation or collection kind. Refuse unsupported transformations; a future copy/catch-up/cutover strategy would require its own explicit data-preservation design. An explicit drop is irreversible with respect to document data; recreating metadata is not a rollback.

For views, retain `viewOn` and ordered pipelines, and extract namespace dependencies from supported `$lookup`, `$graphLookup`, `$unionWith` and nested pipelines. Handle shared collection/view namespaces and cycles. Unknown dependency-bearing constructs cannot silently produce a complete graph; require sufficient explicit evidence or refuse dependent destructive changes. [`$out`/`$merge` are not standard view definitions](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/collmod/); materialization belongs to authored data work, not a view-creation fallback.

## 8. Native migration artifacts and document migrations

Introduce/reuse a **generic provider-native migration representation** in the host workflow. It must carry format/version, provider identity, migration identity, ordered unit IDs, required features, checksums, typed payloads, assertions, recovery/reverse information and source locations. The format registration mechanism is generic; BSON decoding stays in the plugin.

A readable MongoDB encoding can use `.mongodb.json` plus Extended JSON payloads; finalize naming against #4204. Do not store JSON in `.sql`, wrap it in fake SQL statements/comments, or require a SQL lexer to discover/split/hash it. Rendering to SQL must explicitly refuse. Human-readable plans expose resource, operation, relevant before/after state, risk and execution boundaries alongside the full accepted native artifact.

The first native document-operation vocabulary should cover explicit inserts, filtered updates (including supported update pipelines), filtered deletes, and bounded read assertions. Each operation declares its target namespaces, scope/bounds, relevant options, expected results, failure behavior and retry classification. Schema commands use typed planned operations, not an unrestricted hidden `runCommand` escape hatch.

No arbitrary JavaScript, server-side code execution, hidden shell programs, or unconstrained administrative commands are required. Unsupported operators and namespace-changing/data-output stages must be rejected rather than bypass dependency, protected-resource or approval checks. Disabling document validation requires a visible explicit operation option and policy decision, never a global hidden convenience.

### Bounded execution and restart

[MongoDB `updateMany`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.updatemany/) is atomic per document, not across the whole matching set. Partial modifications survive failure. A successful schema diff also says nothing about whether a business-data migration completed.

Provide bounded batches, progress and durable checkpoints for the supported long-running backfill path. Define selection/resume-key assumptions, BSON ordering, operation and time budgets, original-filter rechecks and terminal verification. Do not pretend `updateMany` has a global row-limit guarantee or that a preflight count prevents concurrent writers expanding its scope.

Resume only when idempotence or transactional/checkpoint evidence justifies it. A generic `idempotent = true` declaration does not prove safety; retain the author's responsibility and the actual mechanism. Non-idempotent increments, appends or generated values must not be blindly replayed after an unknown outcome.

A document `schemaVersion` field is optional **application-owned data**, not Ptah's migration-history version. Never inject it automatically. A schema fingerprint excludes ordinary data, so bind document-migration preconditions and postconditions separately and state the concurrent-writer assumptions. Online guarantees need cooperating writers or an explicit write window; this plugin is not a general ETL/CDC orchestrator.

Generated reverse schema operations, authored compensating data operations, and actual transaction rollback are different concepts. Do not promise a `down` migration can restore dropped documents, expired data or overwritten values that were never captured.

## 9. Sessions, history, locks, and uncertain outcomes

Use #4204's session handles and history policy. Keep clients, sessions, cursors and transactions inside the provider. Require an explicit target database; do not confuse `authSource` with it or silently migrate the driver's default database. Use the native URI parser for replica-set/SRV/TLS/auth options, redact credentials and distinguish authentication from namespace/DDL authorization.

### Transaction boundaries

MongoDB [permits some collection/index creation inside transactions under restrictions](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/transactions-operations/); it does not provide a universal transaction around an arbitrary metadata migration. Initial metadata plans should expose non-atomic units unless a particular transactional strategy is explicitly implemented and tested. Reject a requested all-or-nothing mode that cannot be honored.

Bounded document transactions on supported replica sets may share their session with the corresponding history/checkpoint writes where the engine permits. Ordinary inspection must not be pushed inside a transaction that forbids `listCollections`/`listIndexes`. Configure/test supported write/read concerns and driver retry behavior; an RPC batch or a transaction callback is not an exactly-once guarantee.

### Storage primitives, not another migrator

Use protected MongoDB collections to implement the host's revision/step/checkpoint and lock contracts. Initialization is a visible mutation step, never a side effect of inspect/plan. Store migration and step identities, immutable input digest, provider semantic identity, known progress/outcomes and recovery evidence under host policy. Do not put TTL on revision/checkpoint evidence.

Scope cooperative locking to the actual managed database/resources, not just a source directory. Contending projects must not independently mutate the same namespace. Use atomic conditional ownership changes and owner-checked renew/release operations, with documented durability and failover semantics.

**A TTL index is not a mutex, and an expired lease is not proof the former executor stopped.** A token stored in a lock/history document does not fence a separately issued MongoDB DDL command. On lease loss, stop dispatch; on uncertain ownership or an in-flight write, fail closed. Do not permit automatic takeover/replay unless the former executor is conclusively stopped or fenced and outstanding outcomes are reconciled. Re-reading metadata alone does not prevent a paused former owner from resuming later. A first implementation may use durable non-expiring ownership with explicit recovery rather than claim safe automatic failover from a TTL lease. Document stale-owner recovery and test a paused former owner resuming after another process attempts takeover.

The lock coordinates cooperating Ptah executions; it cannot prevent external application/admin changes. Treat standalone durability and replica-set failover guarantees separately.

### Recovery and approval binding

Preserve #4204's outcomes: not started, running, confirmed applied/not applied/rolled back, known partial failure, and outcome unknown. A timeout, plugin death, cancelled context or lost reply after dispatch does not prove rollback. No automatic whole-migration retry.

After ambiguity, inspect the relevant full definitions/UUIDs and durable history before resuming. Object-name existence alone is insufficient evidence that the exact requested operation succeeded. Where evidence cannot determine the result, retain an unresolved status and require explicit recovery rather than manufacture success.

Bind accepted plans to provider semantic identity/build policy, payload/fingerprint versions, exact units, target database identity, relevant UUIDs/metadata, capabilities/FCV and declared data preconditions. Resolve source variables before approval. Provider changes, target recreation or relevant drift invalidate the plan; credentials and confidential query results do not enter artifacts/logs.

## 10. Search / Vector Search extension design

Do not bake in the assumption that these require only an Atlas Administration HTTP API: the [Go driver exposes search-index management](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/go/current/indexes/), and actual availability depends on the deployment. They are a separate object family with their own inspection/coverage and capability profile.

A later implementation should cover typed search/vector definitions, names and types, mappings/analyzers or vector dimensions/similarity/quantization, exact definition comparison, create/update/drop and referenced-collection dependencies. Model unsupported/unknown fields explicitly, including features that trigger external embedding work or cost.

[`listIndexes` excludes Search indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/listindexes/); use the dedicated listing surface. [Search index management is asynchronous](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/php-library/v1.x/reference/method/mongodbcollection-createsearchindex/): acceptance of a request is not successful/queryable completion. Require bounded polling, observed desired definition, readiness/version evidence, explicit failure/timeout handling and restart reconciliation. An old definition remaining queryable must not count as successful application of a new definition.

Keep deployment provisioning, embedding generation/backfill and application query cutover out of this object reconciler. This extension is an architectural test for generic long-running native operations, not permission to bypass Ptah's plan/history boundary. Its full implementation is not required to close the first-delivery scope above.

## 11. Verification and documentation

Test the **packaged subprocess path** through the public SDK, not only helper functions in the plugin repository.

Required suites include:

- Native-only schemas/plans with no relational objects; fixture and real plugin add native kinds without editing host semantic switches; source-to-plan-to-apply-to-inspect round trips and repeated empty diffs.
- Compound key ordering; literal BSON document order; exact numeric/BSON types; missing/null/default distinctions; duplicate keys; codec/fingerprint stability; text/wildcard normalization; shared namespace collisions and case/dot-containing names.
- Validators against heterogeneous pre-existing data; strict versus moderate; explicit weakening/bypass; 9.0 constraint preparation/success/failure/rule change and older-version/FCV refusal.
- Ordinary index families/options and invalid combinations; duplicate/null/partial unique cases; hidden unique/TTL behavior; in-place TTL changes; replacement conflicts; irreversible-effect reports; standard-view dependencies and cycles.
- Permission-limited/name-only inspection, multi-batch cursor failure, unknown collection/index state, unmanaged resources and protected internal/history resources. No destructive plan from incomplete coverage.
- Interrupted data batches, idempotent versus non-idempotent replay, concurrent writers, checkpoint recovery, data assertions, transaction-mode refusal and correct history coupling.
- Competing Ptah processes, stale/paused owners, lease loss, primary stepdown, timeout and crash after server acceptance but before history/reply; no fabricated success, rollback or automatic takeover.
- Missing/untrusted/incompatible plugin; offline help/decode behavior; secrets/TLS/auth failures; subprocess stdout/LSP framing; fresh external-module builds, installed-package discovery and cleanup.

Use pinned standalone and replica-set fixtures; do not infer failover evidence from a single-node development replica set. Sharded/deployment-restricted negative tests must prevent unsupported writes. Record Atlas evidence separately from local Community/Enterprise evidence; credentials and cloud spend are explicit CI inputs, never required to build the host.

Build/import gates prove that `ptah`, `ptah-compat` and `ptah-ls` retain `CGO_ENABLED=0` builds and that their module/dependency graphs do not contain the plugin or MongoDB/BSON-only dependencies. Record inspect/plan/apply overhead and RPC counts; metadata and document batches must remain bounded.

Publish runnable guides for installation/configuration, connection/auth/TLS and required privileges by workflow, schema inventory/adoption, HCL/BSON types, first migration, schema versus document changes, validator rollout, index risks, native artifacts, transactions/history, uncertain-outcome recovery and the exact support matrix. Include a complete expand/backfill/contract example and the missing-plugin -> setup link -> successful rerun flow. Examples run in CI. Clearly separate unsupported engine behavior, implementation gaps and unverified deployments.

## 12. Delivery sequence and definition of done

1. **Native-only seam and ADR:** map this design onto #4204, close generic source/artifact/history/coverage gaps, publish the operation/version matrix and record source/test baselines. No second pipeline or pre-refactor compatibility work.
2. **Read/declare/compare slice:** external repository, driver/session setup, registration and offline codecs/descriptors, accurate inspection/export and native-only diff/plan with no mutation hidden in analysis.
3. **Metadata execution:** required collections, validators, ordinary indexes and views; exact native units, host history/locks, safe non-atomic execution and recovery; real repeat-to-no-diff tests.
4. **Document migrations:** versioned native artifacts, bounded mutations/assertions/backfills, progress/checkpoints, explicit retry/transaction/reverse semantics and rollout example.
5. **Release:** full subprocess conformance, fault tests, independent artifacts, optional install flow, setup/catalog documentation and measured capability evidence. Preserve explicit extension boundaries for advanced collection kinds, Search/Vector Search, sharding and security/control-plane work.

Completion requires:

- [ ] The implementation lives in `stokaro/ptah-mongodb-plugin`, is separately installable and is not embedded or bundled by default.
- [ ] Only #4204's public SDK/protocol and neutral contracts are used; host/SDK dependency and CGO gates pass.
- [ ] Native-only schema and migration workflows reach the actual Ptah pipeline, with one planner/history policy and no fake SQL or parallel document core.
- [ ] Collection/index/view/validator semantics, ordered BSON, identity, source positions, coverage and deterministic normalization survive decode -> inspect -> compare -> plan -> execute -> export.
- [ ] The required metadata and versioned document workflows work against the declared pinned server/FCV/topology matrix; inspection and plan generation are read-only.
- [ ] Native migration discovery/checksums/status and SQL-only format refusals work; no unsupported file or payload is silently skipped.
- [ ] Unmanaged/unknown/system/history state is preserved or blocks dependent destructive work; no silent collection recreation or automatic data repair.
- [ ] Validator/TTL/unique/index-replacement risks and 9.0 constraint transitions are modeled and tested; data verification is not confused with schema no-diff.
- [ ] Lock contention/loss, partial application, ambiguous outcomes, recovery, stale-plan rejection and bounded backfill replay are tested through real subprocesses.
- [ ] Fresh installation, setup links, missing/incompatible-provider diagnostics, source builds and supported packaged targets are documented and tested.
- [ ] Advanced families have honest inspection/coverage/refusal dispositions and documented extension boundaries, not an unqualified “MongoDB fully supported” claim.

**Non-goals:** MongoSQL/SQL DDL translation; embedding MongoDB in the host; a second plugin system or migrator; legacy Ptah compatibility/import tooling; unrestricted JS/`mongosh` execution; automatic validator inference or business-data repair; general ETL/CDC/copy-and-cutover orchestration; implicit Atlas infrastructure/user management; or untested certification of MongoDB-compatible products.

<!-- local-draft: none, reason: local model down (127.0.0.1:8080 refused the connection); drafted by Claude from the code -->
## Summary

Cache tenant connection-string resolution and the pre-built tenant filter per entity type, to cut per-request overhead in multi-tenant applications.

## Motivation

- **Connection string resolution**: the tenant connection factories run on every scoped request; in many implementations resolving the connection string involves a lookup (configuration, database or external service). Today there are six provider-specific `ITenantConnectionFactory` interfaces (`src/Encina.ADO.SqlServer|PostgreSQL|MySQL/Tenancy/ITenantConnectionFactory.cs` and `src/Encina.Dapper.SqlServer|PostgreSQL|MySQL/Tenancy/ITenantConnectionFactory.cs`), each with `CreateConnectionAsync`, `CreateConnectionForTenantAsync` and `ValueTask<Either<EncinaError, string>> GetConnectionStringAsync(CancellationToken)` (the tenant comes from the ambient tenant context), plus the generic `ITenantConnectionFactory<TConnection>` in `src/Encina.Tenancy/Data/ITenantConnectionFactory.cs` whose `GetConnectionStringAsync(string? tenantId = null, CancellationToken)` takes the tenant. Entity Framework Core and MongoDB have no such factory.
- **Tenant filters**: the ADO tenant-aware repositories rebuild the `WHERE tenant_id = @TenantId` clause on every call through `GetTenantFilterClause()` and `ITenantEntityMapping.IsTenantEntity` (for example `src/Encina.ADO.SqlServer/Tenancy/TenantAwareFunctionalRepositoryADO.cs`); the result depends only on the entity mapping, so it is cacheable. Entity Framework Core uses model-level query filters (built once), so it gains nothing.
- **Impact**: hot paths in high-traffic multi-tenant applications, executed thousands of times per second.
- **Security note**: a connection string is a secret. Storing it in a distributed cache stores a secret in plaintext outside the process, and `AGENTS.md` §3 forbids secrets reaching logs or plaintext storage (Dilemma D1).

## Proposed Solution

### 1. Cache connection strings per tenant

A decorator around the tenant connection factory, opt-in, TTL configurable (default 10 minutes), with a manual invalidation API for tenant configuration changes:

```csharp
public sealed class CachedTenantConnectionFactory : ITenantConnectionFactory
{
    public async ValueTask<Either<EncinaError, string>> GetConnectionStringAsync(CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        // Key: encina:tenant:conn:{tenantId}; only a Right value is cached.
    }
}
```

### 2. Cache the tenant filter per entity type

```csharp
// In-memory only: the filter depends only on the entity mapping, identical across instances.
private static readonly ConcurrentDictionary<Type, string> _filterCache = new();
```

Cache keys:

```
encina:tenant:conn:{tenantId}      // Connection string per tenant
encina:tenant:filter:{entityType}  // In-memory only
```

Where the decorator lives (six provider packages, or once over `Encina.Tenancy`'s generic factory) is part of the plan.

## Alternatives Considered

Settled and trivial choices:

1. **Opt-in** (Settled): nothing is cached unless registered. Citation: `AGENTS.md` §1.
2. **Errors** (Settled): a `Left` from the inner factory is returned and never cached; a cache failure falls back to the inner factory. Citation: `AGENTS.md` §3 (ROP; background failures not swallowed).
3. **Secrets** (Settled): the cached connection string never reaches logs, activity tags or health-check output. Citation: `AGENTS.md` §3 (secret handling, #851).
4. **Time** (Trivial): TTL by the cache provider's expiration; any clock via `TimeProvider`.
5. **Provider coherence** (Settled): the behaviour is the same for the six ADO/Dapper packages. Citation: `AGENTS.md` §5; the filter half applies only where a filter clause is built (ADO) and is not applicable to Entity Framework Core and MongoDB.

Dilemma D1: Where are connection strings cached? Option A, `ICacheProvider` (distributed): resolution done once for the whole fleet; wins when resolution calls an external service and many instances start together, but stores secrets outside the process and needs encryption or access control on the cache. Option B, `IMemoryCache` (local): the secret stays in process memory; wins when resolution is a database or configuration lookup per instance and the secret must not leave the process, at the cost of one resolution per instance and tenant. Option C, selectable by option, defaulting to local: wins when both shapes are real.

Dilemma D2: Is the filter half worth building? Option A, build it now with a benchmark showing the clause build cost: wins if the benchmark proves a measurable share of request time. Option B, drop it from this issue and keep only the connection string cache: wins if the clause is a cheap string concatenation (to be measured), avoiding a static cache that must also be bounded and tested for every provider.

## Affected Packages

- [ ] Encina (core)
- [ ] Encina.EntityFrameworkCore
- [x] Encina.Dapper.*
- [x] Encina.ADO.*
- [ ] Encina.AspNetCore
- [ ] Encina.MongoDB
- [ ] Encina.OpenTelemetry
- [x] Encina.Caching.*
- [ ] Encina.Messaging
- [ ] Encina.Polly
- [ ] Encina.Cdc
- [x] Other: `Encina.Tenancy` (generic `ITenantConnectionFactory<TConnection>`)

## Provider Implementation Matrix

Category: Database, six packages carry a connection factory today; Entity Framework Core and MongoDB have none, so they are not applicable. SQLite is out of the matrix (ADR-024).

| Provider | Connection string cache | Filter cache | Notes |
|----------|:-:|:-:|-------|
| ADO-SqlServer | yes | yes (if D2 keeps it) | |
| ADO-PostgreSQL | yes | yes (if D2 keeps it) | |

## Cross-Cutting Integration

> Per `AGENTS.md` §6 (Cross-cutting integration check): Every new feature MUST be evaluated against ALL 12 transversal functions.

| 1 | **Caching** (`ICacheProvider`, decorator, `[Cache]`) | Integrate | The feature. |

| 11 | **Module Isolation** (`ModuleId`, `IModuleContext`) | Not applicable | Tenant connections are not module-scoped. |
| 12 | **Audit Trail** (`IOperationAuditStore`, audit events) | Not applicable | |

items.title: A fieldMapping reading spec.<name> for the path parameter <name> deletes the property it reads from, and the kind becomes unusable
items.body:
## Searchable symptoms

```
strict decoding error: unknown field "spec.<name>"
refusing to request ...: unresolved path parameter(s) [<name>] -- the value is absent, so this
  request would address the literal template rather than a resource
```

Plus the silent form: a chart renders `spec.<name>: <value>` on a CR, `kubectl apply` **succeeds**, and `kubectl get -o yaml` does not show the field. Nothing reports that it was dropped.

## What happens

A request-direction mapping whose source is the spec property with **the same name as the path parameter it fills** causes the generator to delete that property — so the mapping's own source no longer exists.

```yaml
identifiers: [node_id]
- action: create
  method: PUT
  path: /v1/nodes/{node_id}/states/provision
  requestFieldMapping:
    - inPath: node_id
      inCustomResource: spec.node_id      # <- points at the property the suppression removes
```

Generated spec properties: `clean_steps, configdrive, configurationRef, target`, `required: [configurationRef, target]`. **`node_id` is absent.**

Then at runtime the mapping reads `spec.node_id`, finds nothing, and **silently skips** — `go/rest-dynamic-controller/internal/tools/client/builder/builder.go:215-217`:

```go
val, found, err := pathparsing.GetNestedField(...)
if err != nil || !found { continue }
```

No parameter, no error, no log line. `buildPath` then leaves the literal `{node_id}`, and the request is refused at `go/rest-dynamic-controller/internal/tools/client/restclient.go:166` (and the identical guard at `:691`). **So the kind cannot execute that verb at all.**

## Why this is a generation bug and not an unsatisfiable config

Two hypotheses were live and they need different fixes, so this was settled by measurement rather than argument:

- **H1** — path-only parameters never become spec fields, so `inCustomResource: spec.<name>` is simply unsatisfiable for a path parameter and belongs rejected at admission.
- **H2** — the parameter *does* become a spec field and the suppression removes it, i.e. the rule deletes what it reads from.

**H1 is refuted and H2 confirmed by an existing, passing test** — `internal/tools/oas2jsonschema/path_item_parameters_test.go`, `TestPathItemParameters_BecomeSpecFields`. Its inputs separate the axes, which is what makes it decisive: `realm` is declared **only** as a path-item parameter, is **absent from the request body** (which carries only `username`), and the file contains **zero** mapping references. It asserts `realm` is both a spec property and in `required`. So a path-only parameter with no mapping reaches the spec as required; the mapping is what removes it.

Confirmed across a consumer's four real kinds, where the discriminator is whether the mapping's source **name** differs from the parameter's:

| kind | mapping | `node_id`/`uuid` in the generated spec |
|---|---|---|
| `BaremetalNode` | `uuid` ← `spec.name` (different name) | both `name` and `uuid` present |
| `Port` | `uuid` ← `status.uuid` | `node_uuid` present |
| `NodePower` | `node_id` ← `spec.node_id` (**same name**) | **absent** |
| `NodeProvision` | `node_id` ← `spec.node_id` (**same name**) | **absent** |

The field name is `requestFieldMapping` (deprecated, `json:"requestFieldMapping"`, `types.go:555`), which is **normalized into the unified `FieldMappingItem` at load time** by `toDomainFieldMapping` (`internal/tools/render/helper.go:17`, legacy loop `:46-53`) — which is why the suppression sees it. `fieldMapping` (`types.go:562`) behaves the same.

## The other half: the mapping is trusted twice and checked neither time

Enumerated by `git grep '\.Parameters\['` across rest-dynamic-controller — exactly four writers, no fifth. Precedence, highest first: **`fieldMapping` > `requestFieldMapping` > Configuration CR `spec.path.<action>` > CR spec > CR status.**

- CR **spec** and **status** are gated on the parameter being declared in the document (`builder.go:516`, via `ReqParams` from `clienttools.go:567`, merging path-item and operation params at `:590`).
- **`requestFieldMapping` and `fieldMapping` are not gated at all** — a mapping can fill a placeholder the document never declares, and can name a source that does not exist, with neither checked.

So a mapping is trusted both to supply a parameter and to find its source. The self-referential case is where those two trusts collide.

## Suggested fix — the clearest form, not the cheapest

A **generation-time** check: a request-direction mapping whose `inCustomResource` names a `spec.` path must leave that path present in the generated spec. Two cases fall out:

1. **The source is the parameter's own name** → the suppression must not fire. Removing the property would delete the mapping's source, so the author's declaration is self-defeating and the property has to survive. This is the reported case.
2. **The source is some other `spec.` path that does not exist** in the generated spec → report it. The author has named a field nobody can set.

This belongs at generation, where the author can still act on it, rather than at admission (which cannot see the document) or at runtime (where it is a refused request three layers from the cause).

It is the same shape as #412: a rule asserting that the paths a mapping or transform reads are contained in the schema it reads them from.

## What is NOT established, and should not be folded in

The consumer observed six machines transition `available → active` through these exact kinds, which the code above says should have been **refused**. That is unresolved: the guard at `restclient.go:166` shipped in `efbf36b` and `git tag --contains` gives `0.48.0, 0.49.0, 0.50.0`, so it **was** active in the version they ran, and the Configuration-CR route is structurally impossible for these two kinds (no `configurationFields` entry, therefore no `path` property on the generated Configuration CRD). The remaining possibilities are that `spec.node_id` was present on CRs written before the schema changed — in which case **a write to any of them prunes the field and breaks it**, since admission prunes on write — or that the transitions did not go through these kinds at all. The deciding datum is a stored CR object, which was never captured.

That open question does not affect this bug's existence; it is recorded here so nobody reads "it works in practice" as evidence against the mechanism.

## Also observed in the same render

`status field 'node_id' not found in response, defaulting to string` — fired correctly. `identifiers: [node_id]` cannot populate `status.node_id` here, because `populateStatusFields` (`internal/controllers/helpers.go:97`) reads only an API **response body**, the findby items carry no `node_id`, and the PUT returns 202 with no body. So the generator was already reporting that half.

items.body:
> **Audit design `d20260916-1`** — critère `ds:confiance` · impact **fort** (`P1`)

## La référence

CDC §5.1 Principes de protection des données ; docs/design/appointments/wireframes.md — Étape 4

## Ce qu'elle prescrit

CDC §5.1 : « Consentement et finalités. Information claire des utilisateurs, base légale explicite pour chaque traitement (notifications, marketing ultérieur). » Le wireframe de l'étape 4 dessine « [ ] J'accepte les CGV et la politique de données — consentement RGPD explicite ».

## Ce que l'écran fait

L'étape « Vos coordonnées » demande prénom, nom, e-mail, téléphone et un champ libre où le jeu d'essai montre des données de santé (« Allergie aux huiles essentielles d'agrumes »). Aucune case de consentement, aucun lien vers une politique de données, aucune mention des finalités — alors que l'e-mail et le SMS servent à des envois automatisés. Même absence sur /spa-lumiere/compte/inscription.

## La direction proposée

Ajouter à l'étape 4 et au formulaire d'inscription une mention des finalités avec lien vers la politique de données, et la case de consentement prescrite, bloquante pour la soumission.

## Portée

L'écart se retrouve à l'identique sur :

- `C:/Program Files/Git/spa-lumiere/compte/inscription`

## Preuve

```
360 px, étape « Coordonnées » complète, et /spa-lumiere/compte/inscription
```

![Les cinq champs de l'étape 4 : rien entre le dernier champ et les boutons](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TMap-Works/spa-booking/qa-captures/docs/design/captures/d20260916-1/a9433d1ab360-1.png)
